items.quote: How, and with what Vertue, Physick worketh upon Mans body and cureth his Diseases
items.what: CHAP. IV. How, and with what Vertue, Physick worketh upon Mans body and cureth his Diseases
items.note: The chapter heading announces its one subject: how and by what vertue physick works on the body and cures.

items.quote: That which Physitians commonly dispute and contend for
items.what: That which Physitians commonly dispute and contend for
items.note: The text sets apart one question as the common dispute of physitians: cure by contraries or by like.

items.quote: according to Hippocrates his Maxim, that Contraryes are to be cured with CONTRARYES
items.name: Hippocrates
items.note: The maxim that contraries are cured with contraries is given to Hippocrates.

items.quote: or Like with LIKE, according to Paracelsus
items.name: Paracelsus
items.note: The maxim that like is cured with like is given to Paracelsus.

items.quote: In lib. de flatibus.
items.name: lib. de flatibus
items.note: The margin note names a writing beside the sentence that gives the two maxims; the mark stands before the naming of Hippocrates his Maxim.

items.quote: these Maxims may be both received in the Anatomy of Nature, though they seem thwart one the other
items.note: The author holds that both maxims can be accepted, though they seem to cross each other.

items.quote: many attaine not the Mind of Phylosophers, which to them seems to be at variance, because they cannot understand how to reconcile them by a seasonable and sutable interpretation
items.note: The text says the philosophers' meaning is missed by many and that their seeming disagreement is removed by interpretation: their words are not to be taken as they first stand.

items.quote: Physick is nothing else but an opposition of those things that are desired, to wit, a refreshing of the strength and Balsom, and a removing of superfluityes or impurities that cause diseases
items.note: The text says what Physick is: refreshing strength and Balsom, and removing the superfluities or impurities that cause diseases.

items.quote: hunger is to to be cured with meat, thirst with drink, fulnesse with evacuation, inanition with reflection, labour with rest, idlenesse with labour
items.name: Hippocrates
items.note: Examples of cure by contraries given as the saying of Hippocrates, with the general rule that follows them.

items.quote: Paracelsus therefore doth not find fault with Hippocrates
items.name: Paracelsus
items.note: The author reports that Paracelsus does not object to Hippocrates' saying that contraries cure contraries.

items.quote: he is poynt blanck against Galen, who applyed that Contrariety of Hippocrates chiefly to those bare and naked qualityes which Hippocrates utterly disclaimed
items.name: Paracelsus
items.note: Paracelsus is reported as flatly against Galen, who is said to have applied Hippocrates' contrariety to bare qualities that Hippocrates disclaimed.

items.quote: he by an unhappy mistake referred the first and principall Idaea's of Cures to Refrigerations, Calefactions, Humectations, Exsiccations, with their companions
items.name: Galen
items.note: A view reported in order to reject it: cures referred to cooling, heating, moistening and drying. The sentence says only he; the nearest person named before it is Galen. The text calls it an unhappy mistake.

items.quote: those Hippocraticall vertues are they which doe the cures, the Physitian is but the minister or servant
items.note: The natures of medicines, also called Hippocraticall vertues, do the cures; the physitian only serves.

items.quote: The onely and alone NATURES of Physicall medicines, as hath been said
items.note: The words as hath been said point back to an earlier place in this writing; the lines given do not show which.

items.quote: this very selfe same Nature, which is our Life and Balsom, or balsomicall Mummy, that preserveth the body from all corruption
items.note: Nature is here said to be our Life and Balsom, or balsomicall Mummy, which keeps the body from corruption.

items.quote: the Saline moysture, that is, of the inferiour Balsom springing up in the inferiour from the superiour
items.note: The Saline moysture is explained as the inferiour Balsom, which springs up in the inferiour from the superiour.

items.quote: is its own proper Physitian in Mans body, who asketh nothing of the outward Physitian but Instauration
items.note: Our own Nature is the proper physitian in the body; it asks of the outward physitian only Instauration.

items.quote: Instauration, or as tis commonly called, fortification applyed to the diseased part by a most pure medicine
items.note: Instauration is given its common name, fortification, and is said to be applied to the diseased part by a most pure medicine.

items.quote: which sometimes worketh wonders, when the Physitians to their great disgrace and shame of their Profession could doe no good
items.note: The author says Nature sometimes works wonders where the physitians could do nothing and had given the patient up.

items.quote: the Medicinall Balsom like a coadjutour or privy counsellour assisteth the Vitall or Radicall and Naturall Balsom because of the simpathy and common agreement between them
items.note: Two Balsoms are set apart: the Medicinall one from outside helps the Vitall, Radicall and Naturall one within, by the simpathy between them.

items.quote: which being restored it is of it selfe able as an inward and unknown Antidote to chase all its enemies out of its Monarchy by the onely power of the Vitall facultyes
items.note: Once the natural strength is restored, it drives out its enemies by its own power, as an inward and unknown Antidote.

items.quote: Nature cureth with like things.
items.note: The margin note sums the paragraph as cure by like things.

items.quote: To go about to cure a disease with contrary qualities, is to raise and stir up intrinsick commotions to the utter overthrow of Nature
items.note: The author rejects cure by contrary qualities: it stirs up inward commotion and overthrows a Nature already weakened.

items.quote: Contraryes will not willingly entertertaine each other
items.note: A further reason against cure by contraries: contraries do not receive each other.

items.quote: where there is no true action and passion, there can follow no true Naturall effect
items.note: Where two things neither work on nor suffer from each other, the author says no true natural effect follows.

items.quote: medicines should not be contrary to the grieved part, but very agreeable to it, and have the same Externall Nature (because of the Harmony between the great and little world) as the place affected hath the Inward
items.note: The medicine should agree with the affected part and have outwardly the same Nature the part has inwardly; the reason given is the Harmony of the great and little world.

items.quote: Man is therefore called a Microcosm or little world, because the whole world preserveth, nourisheth and cureth him
items.note: The text says why man is called Microcosm or little world: the whole world preserves, nourishes and cures him.

items.quote: When the fruits of the Earth, Aire, Water and Fire of the Microcosm are sick, they must be restored by fruits like themselves of the Macrocosm
items.note: The sick fruits of the four elements in man are restored by like fruits of the great world.

items.quote: Nature strengthened and assisted by its own Nature doth more forcibly drive out all its enemyes, seeing every Nature is Naturally the best preserver of it selfe
items.note: Nature helped by its own Nature drives out its enemies more strongly; each Nature best preserves itself.

items.quote: it alone being the genuine Physitian of all diseases, as Galen witnesseth in his 13 Book of Method
items.name: Galen
items.note: Galen, in his 13 Book of Method, is called as witness that Nature alone is the genuine physitian of all diseases.

items.quote: It is the First Mover of every cure, without whose strength and vigour all Physick is in vaine and to no purpose
items.note: Nature is named the First Mover of every cure; without it all Physick is in vain.

items.quote: Nature continued in its Temperature is in it selfe medicinable, and it selfe healeth its own infirmities by the innate Mummy
items.note: Nature kept in its Temperature heals its own infirmities by the innate Mummy.

items.quote: every thing by a kind of naturall instinct desireth to be perfected and preserved
items.note: The author gives as well known that every thing desires its own preservation and abhors its destruction.

items.quote: those that are wounded perceive a presentaneous succour from Nature as of one hastening to helpe
items.note: Daily experience of wounds is brought as proof: Nature hastens to help and does not rest till the wound is cured.

items.quote: some say that contraryes are to be cured by Contraryes, they are not much mistaken if they have not respect to the qulaityes, but the vertues of a contrary Nature
items.name: some
items.note: The saying of unnamed some is allowed on one condition: that it be meant of vertues of a contrary Nature, not of qualities.

items.quote: there are as many crosse and hurtfull vertues to nature as there be good and healthfull for it
items.note: The author sets two kinds of vertues against each other: hurtful ones that work to destroy Nature and good ones that preserve it.

items.quote: contrary qualityes, are not rooted out by contrary quallityes, but rather are irritated and provoked to strife by each other
items.note: Contrary qualities do not remove each other but provoke strife, by which Nature is weakened.

items.quote: Nature is not a quality but a vertue
items.note: The text says what Nature is and is not: a vertue, not a quality; it is therefore helped by vertues.

items.quote: Nature her selfe (who is the Internall Mummy or inward Balsom)
items.note: Nature is said in a bracket to be the Internall Mummy or inward Balsom.

items.quote: when her own inward strength fayleth shee is to be supplyed with outward helpe by her servant the Physitian
items.note: It is Nature, not the physitian, that hunts out the disease; the physitian is her servant and supplies outward help when her inward strength fails.

items.quote: sometimes it may be the best medicine not to use any medicine at all but to leave the ooperation to the sole Archaeus or Art of Nature
items.note: The author allows that the best medicine is sometimes none, the work being left to Nature alone.

items.quote: the sole Archaeus or Art of Nature
items.note: Archaeus is paired by or with Art of Nature, as another name for the same thing.

items.quote: The Inward Physitian doth the work, when the Naturall Physitian faileth.
items.note: The margin note sets an Inward Physitian against a Naturall Physitian that fails. The paragraph beside it calls Nature the inward one and the physitian her servant; the lines given do not say who the note's Naturall Physitian is.

items.quote: it is not by the coldnesse of Opium, but but by the Specifick venemous vertue of the Opium which hath a greater degree of poyson then the occult venomous power of that Pestilence
items.note: The example of Opium in a pestilence: it preserves by its specific venomous vertue, a stronger poison than that of the pestilence, not by its quality of coldness.

items.quote: Thus Nature destroyeth one poyson by another, it subdueth a weak evill by a stronger
items.note: Nature fights with hurtful as well as healthful weapons: one poison destroys another.

items.quote: without vertue the quallity is dead and wholly accidentall
items.note: A quality without vertue is dead and accidental and can give no life or substance, which the medicine must give; one quality does not destroy another, as winter and summer only give place.

items.quote: Roots of diseases in the body of Man are neither hot nor cold
items.note: The roots of diseases are neither hot nor cold.

items.quote: those Accidents and Excrements are but the signes of the disease, and not the disease it selfe
items.note: Heat and cold in a disease are called accidents and excrements: signs of the disease, not the disease.

items.quote: do not spring out of the matter of the body, or out of the four Humours, but from the Nature of the Seed or Astra's and Invisible mechanick Spirits of the Three principles
items.note: The worst diseases are said to come not from the body's matter or the four Humours but from the Seed or Astra's and invisible mechanick Spirits of the Three principles.

items.quote: which Spirits also build their outward house and habitation with shells
items.note: The same invisible Spirits are said to build their own outward house with shells.

items.quote: These Forgers and Invisible Astra's of diseases were not knowne to the Ancients.
items.note: The text says these Forgers and invisible Astra's of diseases were unknown to the Ancients.

items.quote: Physick is a Spirit (not a body) which the Magician or wise man only can discerne
items.note: Physick is said to be a Spirit, not a body, which only the Magician or wise man can discern: a thing open to some only. Magician is paired by or with wise man.

items.quote: the body or Earth of Simples is to be cast away
items.note: A step of work: the body, also called Earth, of the Simples is thrown away.

items.quote: the vertue Heaven or Astrum of it only to be taken
items.note: The other half of the same step: only the vertue, also called Heaven or Astrum, of the Simple is kept. The text does not say here how the two are parted beyond the word sepration that follows.

items.quote: it is necessary that the life should worke upon the life, and the Spirit upon the Spirit by sepration of the impure body, as the intangible Sun Melteth Snow and causeth it to vanish away
items.note: In man and in medicine life must work on life and Spirit on Spirit, with the impure body separated; the likeness given is the sun melting snow.

items.quote: Such is the Nature of all Secrets that they worke without the matter and body because the diseases also are not bodyes
items.note: The text uses Secrets as a name for a kind of medicine and says they work without matter and body, because diseases are not bodies.

items.quote: This is the true and lively Anatomy.
items.note: What has just been said (life working on life, Spirit on Spirit, without the body) is named the true and lively Anatomy.

items.quote: This Mechanick and Forger of diseases is to be subdued and destroyed in his Roote and originall
items.note: The maker of the disease is to be destroyed in its root, not elsewhere.

items.quote: Paracelsus in the Tincture of medicines.
items.name: Paracelsus
items.note: The margin note names Paracelsus and a writing, the Tincture of medicines, beside the sentence on destroying the Forger of diseases in his root.

items.quote: the Mechanick Forger or principle of a Pear's generation hath his habitation in the Roote, not in the branch
items.note: A likeness from trees: the Forger or principle of generation lives in the root, so a tree is destroyed in the seed, not the branch.

items.quote: the grasse which groweth of its own accord is hindred from growing, not by evultion but corruption of the Earth
items.note: A second likeness: grass is stopped not by pulling it up but by corrupting the earth it grows in.

items.quote: See the first Tract of the second book of great Surgery, Degrees and complexions are not considered in diseases.
items.name: the first Tract of the second book of great Surgery
items.note: The margin note sends the reader to a writing, great Surgery, and states that degrees and complexions are not considered in diseases. The note does not name its author.

items.quote: when the Centre, Root, and Seed of diseases are pluckt up and removed the worke is done
items.note: The cure is done when the centre, root and seed of the disease are removed.

items.quote: That Physitian which cureth by complexion is like him that would extinguish the hurtless flame and let alone the fire in the coals
items.note: Cure by complexion is likened to putting out the harmless flame and leaving the fire in the coals; the fire, not the smoke, is to be quenched.

items.quote: in doing the cure the Roote of the seed which containeth the vertues is to be taken in hand
items.note: What springs from the seed is not the disease; the cure takes in hand the root of the seed, which holds the vertues.

items.quote: In his Book of ancient Physick.
items.name: his Book of ancient Physick
items.note: The margin note names a writing beside the sentence on the root of the seed. It says only his; the note itself does not show whose book it is.

items.quote: When Paracelsus saith that like preserve their like, and are destroyed by their contraryes
items.name: Paracelsus
items.note: A saying given to Paracelsus: like preserve their like and are destroyed by their contraries.

items.quote: he doth not meane the first nor second qualityes which he alwayes calleth Recollaceous and invalid ones, but the substance
items.note: Stated: the text says that like and contrary in Paracelsus' saying are not meant of the first or second qualities but of the substance. A gap-only margin note (N192, foreign script) stands at this point.

items.quote: at least the Cherionic, Hippocraticall powers and vertues
items.note: The substance meant is narrowed to the Cherionic, Hippocraticall powers and vertues.

items.quote: first Tract of the second part of his great Chyrurgye, and in other places
items.name: Paracelsus
items.note: The reading of Paracelsus' saying is supported by a place in his great Chyrurgye, the 18. Chap of its first Tract of the second part, and other places not named. A gap stands in the words before the quote.

items.quote: Like things are said to be the Remedies of diseases because they are of the same Anatomy of Nature, and because they have the like Signatures, Qualities and Roots
items.note: The text says in what sense like things are called remedies: same Anatomy of Nature, like Signatures, Qualities and Roots.

items.quote: Contraryes cure because they piece up the defects and wants, because they appease the spirits and consentaneous impurities with a friendly saturity, and because they attempt resolutions, consumptions and tacit ablations
items.note: The text says in what sense contraries cure: they fill up defects, appease the spirits and impurities, and attempt resolutions, consumptions and ablations.

items.quote: Diseases are cured by applying that which is proper for them.
items.note: The margin note sums the paragraph: cure is by what is proper to the disease.

items.quote: That Like are to be preferved with their Like is thus to be understood, viz. that the Salt, Sulphur and Mercury of the Microcosm is preserved by the Salt, Sulphur, and Mercury of the Macrocosm analogically agreeing together
items.note: Stated: the text itself says how like with like is to be understood, as the Salt, Sulphur and Mercury of man preserved by those of the great world, which agree analogically.

items.quote: as in the Microcosm there are various Sulphurs (one of the head, another of the heart, &c.) and various Mercuryes and Salts
items.note: Each of the three is many in man, differing by part of the body (head, heart); the text goes on to say the great world shows a matching variety in herbs and minerals.

items.quote: The ministry of Fire discovereth their agreement, operation, and difference
items.note: Fire is the means by which the agreement, working and difference of these Sulphurs, Salts and Mercuries is found out. The text does not say here how the fire is used.

items.quote: he distributeth all materiall diseases according to those three substances of which our bodies are composed, and according to the excrementitious superfluities arising from meat and drink
items.name: Paracelsus
items.note: A division of diseases by the three substances and by superfluities of food and drink, given to a he. The paragraph does not name him; Paracelsus is the person named in the sentences before (CH4.6) and in N194, so the name here is my inference.

items.quote: as Sulphur may be deprest or heightned four wayes, viz. by the four Elements
items.note: Sulphur can be lowered or raised in four ways, by the four Elements.

items.quote: he called them Sulphurean diseases, such are all Inflamations and Feavers
items.note: Diseases arising from kindled and flaming Sulphur are named Sulphurean; all inflammations and fevers are of this kind.

items.quote: Those that proceed from moysture he Mercuriall.
items.note: Diseases that come from moisture are named Mercuriall.

items.quote: Mercury may three manner of wayes be exalted above the Naturall degree
items.what: three manner of wayes Mercury may be exalted above the Naturall degree
items.note: The text numbers three ways: by heat of an accidental digestive vertue, by heat of exercise and labour, by heat from the Astra's.

items.quote: By the heat of digestion it is distild, and so causeth all sorts of Apoplexies
items.note: Mercury in the body is said to be distild by the heat of digestion, causing apoplexies. A word of work (distild) is used of what happens in the body.

items.quote: by the heat of Excercise it is sublimed
items.note: By the heat of exercise the Mercury is sublimed; madness and frenzy are said to follow.

items.quote: by the heat of the stars it is precipitated, and then causeth the Gout in hands and feet &c. from eating and drinking those things that have too much Tattar in them
items.note: By the heat of the stars the Mercury is precipitated and causes gout; eating and drinking things with too much Tattar is named with it.

items.quote: those diseases that are bred of Salt, he calleh Saline and Nitrons
items.note: Diseases bred of Salt are named Saline and Nitrons, again as what he calls them.

items.quote: Salt destroyeth health 4 wayes, by Resolution, Calcination, (loosing its liquid and humid Temperament) Reverbertion. Alcalization
items.note: Four ways are numbered and named: Resolution, Calcination, Reverbertion, Alcalization. The diseases listed after are ulcers, scabs, tetters, ringworms, itch.

items.quote: all which are diseases arising from the Salt dissolved
items.note: The skin diseases just listed are all put down to dissolved Salt.

items.quote: Surfetting and gluttony which destroy the digestion is the cause of the Salts destruction
items.note: Causes of the Salt's destruction are given: surfeit and gluttony; excess and luxury dissolve it; the stars thrust it out of its degree.

items.quote: Which Salt may be changed and turned into all sorts of Salts, and such as is the Transmutation such also is the disease
items.note: The Salt of man can be turned into every sort of Salt, and the disease follows the kind of change.

items.quote: He saith therefore that the Sulphur kindled in mans body is to be quenched with the Sulphur of the great world, which harmonically agreeth with the other
items.name: Paracelsus
items.note: A saying given to a He: kindled Sulphur in man is quenched with the agreeing Sulphur of the great world. The paragraph does not name him; Paracelsus is my inference from CH4.6 and N194.

items.quote: he that considereth to what end he spake it will find that such a remedy will be contrary to the disease
items.note: Stated: the saying of like Sulphur for Sulphur is to be read by its purpose; so read, the remedy is contrary to the disease.

items.quote: his meaning is, that appropriate Sulphur should be used
items.note: Stated: the Sulphur meant is an appropriate Sulphur, to be found among herbs and minerals, for a feverish fire that is universal and flows from the heart.

items.quote: as Sulphur of Vitriol, Niter, common Salt, and such like
items.what: Sulphur of Vitriol, Niter, common Salt, and such like
items.note: Examples of the appropriate Sulphurs are named: of Vitriol, Niter, common Salt.

items.quote: he saith that Ulcers proceeding from Salts must be cured by Salts
items.name: Paracelsus
items.note: A second saying given to the same he: ulcers that come from Salts are cured by Salts. The name is my inference, as in the items before.

items.quote: if we observe his drift, such Salts are contrary to that which was the cause of the disease, and quite opposite to the disease it selfe
items.note: Stated: read by his drift, the curing Salts are contrary to the cause of the disease and to the disease, though they bear the same name.

items.quote: they are incarnative and consolidative, as Frankencense, Mastick, Myrrhe, Aloes
items.what: Salts that are incarnative and consolidative, as Frankencense, Mastick, Myrrhe, Aloes
items.note: The curing Salts are named by what they do (they make flesh and close up) and by examples.

items.quote: sometime he calls that Salt whatever it be that will melt, and may be resolved into a watry moysture, and then dryed and hardened by Fire, such are the thickned sap and juyces of Trees and Hearbs
items.note: The text says what Salt sometimes means in his usage: anything that melts, dissolves to a watery moisture and is dried and hardened by fire, such as thickened saps and juices. The word Salt is thus not always meant plainly.

items.quote: All Terresterity is the Salt of Paracelsus.
items.note: The margin note says what the Salt of Paracelsus is: all Terresterity.

items.quote: Cumfry cureth the corrosion of Salt.
items.note: The margin note pairs three named things with three faults of the three: Cumfry with the corrosion of Salt, a word with a gap in it with the dissolution of Sulphur, Gold with the too much sublimation of Mercury.

items.quote: Gold thickneth the too much sublimation of Mercury.
items.note: Gold is said to thicken Mercury that is sublimed too much.

items.quote: we are to assist Nature against these impediments which are the causes of diseases
items.note: The margin note says our Nature cures all diseases once impediments are taken away; the impediments are the causes of diseases and the physitian's part is to help Nature against them.

items.quote: there are Three from which all Physick proceedeth, Mercury, Sulphur, Salt
items.what: Three from which all Physick proceedeth, Mercury, Sulphur, Salt
items.note: The three are numbered and named as the source of all Physick.

items.quote: there are three sorts of diseases, Mercuriall, Sulphurean, Saline
items.what: three sorts of diseases, Mercuriall, Sulphurean, Saline
items.note: Diseases are numbered in three sorts matching the three.

items.quote: All Ulcers are cured by incarnating Mercury; All mattery gluish sores by Salt; All Inflamations by Sulphur
items.note: Three rules of cure are given, one for each of the three.

items.quote: All Ulcers are cured by incarnating Mercury
items.note: Here all ulcers are cured by Mercury; in CH4.9 ulcers proceeding from Salts must be cured by Salts, and CH4.8 lists ulcers among diseases arising from the Salt dissolved. The lines given do not reconcile the two.

items.quote: This needs no Reasons to confirme it.
items.note: The author gives the three rules without proof and says none is needed.

items.quote: Medicament though they be contrary to the disease, yet they must of necessity be altogether courteous to Nature
items.note: A medicine may be contrary to the disease but must be friendly to Nature.

items.quote: Medicament though they be contrary to the disease
items.note: CH4.6 says medicines should not be contrary to the grieved part but very agreeable to it; here they may be contrary to the disease. The text speaks of the part in one place and the disease in the other, so the two may agree; recorded for the later step.

items.quote: if she sinck or miscary the Physitian can doe no good
items.note: If Nature fails the physitian can do nothing; CH4.12 adds that if she is kept safe she works incredible wonders.

items.quote: if she abide and be kept safe and sound she worketh incredible wonders
items.note: Nature kept safe works wonders; the two stories that follow are brought in as instances.

items.quote: A stupendious and true Story.
items.note: The margin note sets the account that follows apart as a story and vouches for it as true.

items.quote: As was seen in the New City at Prague, Anno 1602. in a certaine rustick or countryman of Bohemia, whose name was Mathew, about 36 years of age
items.what: what was seen in the New City at Prague, Anno 1602
items.note: The story is fixed by place, year, the man's name and age.

items.quote: he swallowed it so far that it went down quite into his stomack, so that he could by no means get it up againe
items.note: The event: the knife he used to hide in his throat went down into his stomach and could not be got up.

items.quote: by application of drawing Plaisters made of the Load-stone and other things, the poynt of the knife began to force its passage, by a naturall impulse, near the mouth of the stomack
items.note: A step of treatment: drawing plaisters made of Load-stone and other things not named were applied, and the knife's point began to come through near the mouth of the stomach.

items.quote: it was prosperously performed by Florianis Mathis of Brandeburge chiefe Surgion of the Kingdome and City, upon thursday after Whitsunday at seven a clock in the morning
items.note: The knife was cut out by a named surgeon at a stated day and hour, at the man's own request and against the advice of many.

items.quote: The knife was nine fingers breadth transverse in length, his stomack had changed the colour of it just as if it had laine so long in the fire
items.note: The knife's length is given, and that the stomach had changed its colour as fire would have done.

items.quote: it is now laid up among the Emperors rarityes, and hath been shewed as an incredible Miracle to many both in Court and City
items.note: The knife is said to be kept among the Emperors rarityes and shown to many.

items.quote: the Country man could eat and drinke and sleepe, as he told me, without any manner of paine or trouble
items.name: Mathew
items.note: The countryman's own report of his recovery, given to the author in person (as he told me).

items.quote: contrary to the determinate assertion of Physitians Aphorismes
items.name: Physitians Aphorismes
items.note: The recovery is set against what the Physitians Aphorismes assert; the lines given do not quote the assertion.

items.quote: in the year 1606. at Prague a certaine Silesian to get mony did in the presence of many swallow six and forty white flints which he gathered at banck side, weighing almost three Physick pounds
items.what: a second account, in the year 1606. at Prague
items.note: A second story, fixed by year and place: a Silesian swallowed forty-six white flints before many people.

items.quote: all of them being almost four of my handfulls
items.note: The author measures the flints by his own handfuls, speaking as one who handled or saw them.

items.quote: without impairing his health, he went up and down getting his living for many years together, &c.
items.note: The man is said to have lived on unharmed for many years; the account breaks off with &c., and the text given ends here.
